steps.body: Subtracting three-digit numbers runs the same columns backward: ones from ones, tens from tens, hundreds from hundreds.
steps.narration: Subtracting three-digit numbers runs the same columns backward: ones from ones, tens from tens, hundreds from hundreds.

widget.prompt: Show what is LEFT after 486 − 254: build the difference with blocks.
widget.missFeedback: That build names a different number — total each unit's worth and match 500 exactly.
widget.successFeedback: 232 — two hundreds, three tens, two ones, every column paying its own way.

predict.prompt: In 486 − 254, does any column come up short?

options.label: No — each top digit is big enough

predict.reveal: 6 can give 4, 8 can give 5, 4 can give 2 — no column is short, so nothing has to be traded. A column only comes up short when its top digit is smaller than the digit below it, and here every top digit is at least as big.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and watch what each trade does to g3a sub.
invariants: A trade never changes how much there is — ten ones become one ten, one hundred becomes ten tens, and the total stands still while the packaging changes for g3a sub.
misconceptions: Flipping a column to take the small digit from the large one, stranding a carry, or borrowing from a column that has nothing to lend.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If a column comes up short, what must change somewhere else so the total stays exactly the same?

commonErrors.feedback: A ten was borrowed that was never needed — every top digit here is already big enough.
That added the two numbers; the minus sign asks how much is LEFT after taking 361 away.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Work one place at a time, and trade only when a column truly comes up short.
